source.title: Case Study: Interpreting, Manipulating, and Controlling CLIP With Sparse Autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Feature granularity depends on the sparsity setting (L0/L1), not only width

record.tranche_reason: The post reports qualitative observations about feature specificity across sparsity regimes, but does not test the listed claims about size-driven splitting, input partitioning, hierarchies, absorption, canonical units, or objective artifacts.
record.gate_note: The post says its 64x-expansion SAE has multiple similar features and that higher-sparsity SAEs encode subjects more generically. It does not report a controlled dictionary-size sweep or test whether features partition inputs or align geometrically. Feature-visualization tuning values and the k-means activation-mass thresholds are not outcomes for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The post trains one 64x CLIP-image SAE for steering and gives only an unquantified, uncontrolled remark that sparser SAEs have more generic features. There is no dictionary-size sweep, no input-partition or direction comparison, no hierarchy, absorption or cross-size latent analysis, and no objective comparison, so its results do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that images decompose into concepts (k-means groups of SAE features) that can be manipulated as units to steer diffusion models, and that such grouping may be useful for SAEs in other domains.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains one 64x-expansion CLIP-image-embedding SAE and describes a qualitative comparison with higher-sparsity SAEs; it does not reproduce or compare the claim's size-sweep method.
record.method_sensitivity: The post says higher sparsity yields more generic features and fewer features combined for a concept, with higher reconstruction error.

fits_no_version.finding: The author states that sparser SAEs encode subjects more generically, with fewer features per concept and higher reconstruction error. The 64x SAE has several similar but non-redundant features, e.g. for cats.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CLIP-embedding SAEs, lower sparsity (higher L0) yields more fine-grained, nuance-specific features per concept.

record.code_released: not stated (the post links to released weights: https://huggingface.co/gytdau/sae-clip-2)
record.problems: The post says it prioritizes selected samples believed to be interesting and may miss unexpected behavior. The sparsity comparison is qualitative and its settings and measurement procedure are not stated.

untested.parts: All parts: no controlled dictionary-size change, no partition of a coarse feature's inputs, no direction similarity.
All parts: a single CLIP-embedding SAE, with no cross-family or scale comparison of splitting.
All parts: k-means groups of active features are a steering tool, not a test of a hierarchy of split features.
All parts: no parent/child absorption analysis.
All parts: no comparison of latents across SAE sizes.
All parts: no comparison of training objectives and no Matryoshka SAE.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post with no quantitative splitting results. Its sparsity remark concerns L0, not dictionary size, and gives no settings for the comparison run. Gwern's comment about GAN latents was not relevant and was not used.

versions.untested_parts: No controlled increase in dictionary size; no test of whether smaller features are replaced by finer features that partition inputs or lie near the smaller feature's direction.
No test of splitting across large models or open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families, geometric closeness, or a hierarchy of concepts.
No test of parent-child absorption, parent firing where child features activate, or whether size or sparsity changes resolve absorption.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes, decomposition into smaller latents, or novel latents.
The post does not test whether the SAE objective creates splitting on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or test Matryoshka SAEs.
